chapter.title: Design a Key-Value Store
chapter.source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
chapter.primary_goal: Design a distributed key-value store that supports put(key, value) and get(key) while handling big data, high availability, high scalability, automatic scaling, tunable consistency, low latency, replication, conflicts, and failures.

chapter_summary.overview: Chapter 6 begins with the basic key-value data model and the put/get API. It establishes a target system with small key-value objects, large total data volume, high availability, high scalability, automatic scaling, tunable consistency, and low latency. A single-server design is introduced first, but capacity constraints force the move to a distributed key-value store. The chapter then uses CAP to frame the consistency-versus-availability tradeoff during network partitions. The distributed design is built from consistent hashing for partitioning, replication across configurable N replicas, quorum consensus using N/W/R, eventual consistency, vector-clock-based versioning and conflict resolution, gossip-based failure detection, sloppy quorum and hinted handoff for temporary failures, Merkle trees and anti-entropy for permanent failures, cross-data-center replication, and Cassandra-like write/read paths using commit logs, memory cache, SSTables, and Bloom filters.
core_api: put(key, value): insert the value associated with a key.
get(key): retrieve the value associated with a key.
main_design_tradeoffs: Read performance versus write performance versus memory use.
Consistency versus availability during network partitions.
Latency versus consistency through quorum sizes.
Availability versus strict quorum behavior during temporary failures.
Conflict-detection accuracy versus vector-clock metadata growth.

Explain the target requirements and tradeoffs for the chapter's key-value store.
Explain the limits of a single-server in-memory hash-table design and the two optimizations proposed.
Define CAP consistency, availability, and partition tolerance and distinguish CP, AP, and CA.
Explain why a real distributed system must tolerate network partitions and therefore chooses between consistency and availability during a partition.
Explain how consistent hashing partitions data and supports automatic scaling and heterogeneous server capacity.
Explain asynchronous replication across configurable N unique physical servers and cross-data-center placement.
Define N, W, and R and reason about latency/consistency tradeoffs in quorum consensus.
Distinguish strong, weak, and eventual consistency.
Explain versioning, concurrent-write conflicts, and vector clocks.
Determine ancestor versus sibling/conflicting versions from vector clocks.
Explain the two downsides of vector clocks mentioned by the chapter.
Explain gossip-protocol failure detection using membership lists and heartbeat counters.
Explain sloppy quorum and hinted handoff for temporary failures.
Explain anti-entropy and Merkle trees for permanent failure and replica repair.
Explain why cross-data-center replication is needed for data-center outages.
Describe the decentralized system architecture and the coordinator role.
Describe the Cassandra-like write path: commit log, memory cache, then SSTable.
Describe the read path, including memory cache, Bloom filter, SSTables, and returning the result.
Map the chapter's key-value-store goals/problems to the techniques summarized in Table 6-2.

key_value_basics.definition: A key-value store, also called a key-value database, is a non-relational database that stores each unique key with an associated value.
key_requirements: The associated value is accessed through the key.
Keys may be plain text or hashed values.
Short keys are preferable for performance.
key_value_basics.value_treatment: The value is usually treated as an opaque object.

requirements.detail: Scale to support a large data set.
Automatically add/delete servers based on traffic.

single_server_design.basic_approach: Store key-value pairs in an in-memory hash table.
single_server_design.limitation: The complete data set may not fit in memory; a single server reaches capacity quickly.
optimizations: Keep frequently used data in memory and store the rest on disk.
single_server_design.conclusion: A distributed key-value store is required to support big data.

cap_theorem.consistency: All clients see the same data at the same time regardless of which node they connect to.
cap_theorem.availability: Every client requesting data receives a response even if some nodes are down.
cap_theorem.partition_tolerance: The system continues operating despite a communication break between nodes.
cap_theorem.chapter_statement: A distributed system cannot simultaneously provide more than two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
cap_theorem.real_world_note: The chapter says CA cannot exist for real-world distributed applications because network failures are unavoidable and partition tolerance is required.

cap_partition_example.ideal_world: Writes replicate among n1, n2, and n3, so consistency and availability are both achieved when there is no network partition.
cap_partition_example.partition_scenario: n3 cannot communicate with n1 and n2.

CP_choice.behavior: Block writes to n1 and n2 to prevent inconsistency.
CP_choice.cost: The system becomes unavailable for those operations.
CP_choice.example_use_case: Bank systems that require the most up-to-date balance information.

AP_choice.recovery: Synchronize n3 after the partition is resolved.

challenges: Distribute data evenly across multiple servers.
Minimize data movement when nodes are added or removed.
high_level_steps: Place servers on a hash ring.
Hash a key onto the same ring.
Store the key on the first server encountered moving clockwise.

advantages.automatic_scaling: Servers can be added or removed automatically according to load.
advantages.heterogeneity: Assign more virtual nodes to higher-capacity servers and fewer to lower-capacity servers.

data_replication.replication_factor: N, a configurable number of replicas.
selection_rule: Hash the key onto the ring.
Choose the first N unique physical servers.
data_replication.virtual_node_caveat: Multiple virtual nodes may belong to the same physical server, so select unique physical servers rather than simply the first N virtual nodes.
data_replication.data_center_strategy: Place replicas in distinct data centers because an entire data center can fail from power, network, or natural-disaster events.

definitions.W: Write quorum size; a successful write must be acknowledged by W replicas.
definitions.R: Read quorum size; a successful read waits for responses from at least R replicas.

quorum_consensus.coordinator: A node that acts as a proxy between the client and replica nodes.
quorum_consensus.important_note: W = 1 does not mean only one replica receives the data; it means the coordinator needs only one acknowledgement before declaring the write successful.
tradeoffs: W = 1 or R = 1 returns quickly because the coordinator can stop after one replica response.
Larger W or R improves consistency but increases latency because more replica responses must be awaited.
If W + R > N, strong consistency is guaranteed because the read and write quorums overlap.
If W + R <= N, strong consistency is not guaranteed.

configurations.property: Strong consistency because W + R > N

consistency_models.definition: Every read returns the value corresponding to the most recent write; clients never see stale data.
consistency_models.availability_tradeoff: Often requires replicas to block new reads/writes until replicas agree on the current write, which is not ideal for highly available systems.

consistency_models.definition: Subsequent reads may not see the most recent value.
A specific form of weak consistency in which, given enough time, all updates propagate and replicas become consistent.
consistency_models.chapter_choice: Recommended for the chapter's key-value store; Dynamo and Cassandra are cited as adopting eventual consistency.
consistency_models.conflict_implication: Concurrent writes can create inconsistent values, which later require reconciliation.

versioning_and_vector_clocks.versioning: Treat every data modification as a new immutable version.

conflict_example.starting_state: n1 and n2 contain the same original value for name.
concurrent_updates: Server1 changes the value to johnSanFrancisco.
Server2 changes the value to johnNewYork.
conflict_example.result: Two conflicting versions, v1 and v2.

versioning_and_vector_clocks.vector_clock_definition: A [server, version] pair associated with a data item that can determine whether one version precedes, succeeds, or conflicts with another.
figure_6_9_sequence: D2 independently updated by Sz -> D4([Sx, 2], [Sz, 1]).
D3 and D4 conflict; client reconciles and writes D5 through Sx -> D5([Sx, 3], [Sy, 1], [Sz, 1]).

ancestor_rule.rule: X is an ancestor of Y if Y's counters for each participant are greater than or equal to X's corresponding counters.
ancestor_rule.example: D([s0,1],[s1,1]) is an ancestor of D([s0,1],[s1,2]).

downsides: Adds client complexity because the client must perform conflict-resolution logic.
The number of [server, version] pairs can grow quickly.
versioning_and_vector_clocks.metadata_growth_mitigation: Set a vector-clock length threshold and remove the oldest pairs after the limit is exceeded.
versioning_and_vector_clocks.mitigation_tradeoff: Removing old pairs can make descendant relationships impossible to determine accurately, causing reconciliation inefficiency.
versioning_and_vector_clocks.source_note: Page 97 initially says 'vector locks' but the chapter immediately defines and consistently uses vector clocks; this guide preserves the chapter's actual mechanism as vector clocks.

failure_detection.principle: One server's accusation alone is insufficient; usually at least two independent sources are required to mark a server down.

all_to_all_multicasting.assessment: Straightforward but inefficient when many servers exist.

steps: Each node maintains a membership list containing member IDs and heartbeat counters.
Each node periodically increments its own heartbeat counter.
Each node periodically sends heartbeats to random nodes.
Those nodes propagate heartbeat information to other nodes.
Membership lists are updated when heartbeat information is received.
If a member's heartbeat has not increased for a predefined period, the member is considered offline.
gossip_protocol.example: s0 observes that s2's heartbeat does not increase; after other nodes confirm the stale heartbeat, s2 is marked down and the information propagates.

temporary_failures.strict_quorum_issue: Strict quorum can block reads/writes after failures.

sloppy_quorum.behavior: Choose the first W healthy servers for writes and first R healthy servers for reads on the ring; ignore offline servers.

hinted_handoff.behavior: A healthy server temporarily handles operations for an unavailable replica and later hands the changed data back when the failed replica returns.
hinted_handoff.example: s3 temporarily handles reads/writes for unavailable s2, then returns the data to s2 after recovery.

permanent_failures.anti_entropy: Compare replica data and update replicas to the newest versions.

merkle_tree.purpose: Detect inconsistencies while minimizing transferred data.
merkle_tree.definition_summary: A tree where non-leaf hashes are derived from child hashes; it enables efficient verification of large data structures.
construction_steps: Divide the key space into buckets.
Hash each key within a bucket.
Create one hash node per bucket.
Build upward to the root by hashing child nodes.
comparison: If roots match, the replicas contain the same data.
If roots differ, recursively compare child hashes.
merkle_tree.efficiency: Data synchronization volume is proportional to the differences between replicas rather than the total data size.
merkle_tree.scale_example: One possible real-world configuration is 1 million buckets for 1 billion keys, about 1,000 keys per bucket.

data_center_outage.solution: Replicate data across multiple data centers so users can still access data when one entire data center is offline.

features: Clients communicate through get(key) and put(key, value).
A coordinator proxies between the client and the key-value store.
Nodes are placed on a consistent-hashing ring.
The design is completely decentralized so node additions/moves can be automatic.
Data is replicated across multiple nodes.
There is no single point of failure because every node has the same set of responsibilities.

write_path.architecture_basis: The chapter says the write/read paths are primarily based on Cassandra architecture.
steps: Persist the write request to a commit log file.
Save the data in the memory cache.
When memory cache is full or reaches a configured threshold, flush data to an SSTable on disk.
write_path.sstable_definition: A sorted-string table is a sorted list of <key, value> pairs.

read_path.memory_hit: Check memory cache first; if data exists there, return it to the client.
memory_miss_steps: If absent, check the Bloom filter.
Use the Bloom filter to determine which SSTables might contain the key.
Return the result to the client.
read_path.bloom_filter_role: Efficiently identify which SSTables may contain the requested key.

summary_table.technique: Use consistent hashing to spread the load across servers.
Versioning and conflict resolution with vector clocks.

key_concepts.definition: A non-relational database storing unique keys and associated values.
A value whose internal structure is generally not interpreted by the key-value store.
Another term used by the chapter for a distributed key-value store.
The chapter's framework that a distributed system cannot simultaneously provide all three of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
Consistency and partition tolerance while sacrificing availability.
Availability and partition tolerance while sacrificing consistency.
Used to partition data evenly and minimize movement when nodes change.
Number of replicas used to store copies of the data.
Number of replica acknowledgements required for a write to be considered successful.
Number of replica responses required for a read to be considered successful.
A node acting as a proxy between the client and the key-value-store nodes.
A weak consistency model in which replicas converge after updates have had enough time to propagate.
Treating each data modification as a new immutable version.
A collection of [server, version] pairs associated with a data item for reasoning about ancestry and conflicts.
A decentralized failure-detection protocol using membership lists and propagated heartbeats.
Uses the first W/R healthy servers rather than enforcing the strict intended replica set during failures.
A temporary healthy node stores/serves data for an unavailable replica and hands the data back after recovery.
Replica repair by comparing data and updating replicas to the newest version.
A hash tree used to identify inconsistent regions efficiently and minimize replica synchronization traffic.
The durable log to which a write is persisted before the in-memory write path continues.
A sorted list of <key, value> pairs stored on disk.
Used in the read path to identify which SSTables might contain a key.

flashcards.front: What is a key-value store?
flashcards.back: A non-relational database that stores each unique key with an associated value.

flashcards.front: What constraint applies to a key?
flashcards.back: The key must be unique.

flashcards.front: Why are short keys preferred?
flashcards.back: For performance reasons.

flashcards.front: What two APIs must the designed store support?
flashcards.back: put(key, value) and get(key).

flashcards.front: What is the maximum key-value pair size in the requirements?
flashcards.back: Less than 10 KB.

flashcards.front: Name the seven main design characteristics.
flashcards.back: <10 KB pair size, big-data storage, high availability, high scalability, automatic scaling, tunable consistency, low latency.

flashcards.front: What is the simplest single-server implementation?
flashcards.back: An in-memory hash table.

flashcards.front: What two single-server optimizations are proposed?
flashcards.back: Data compression and keeping only frequently used data in memory while storing the rest on disk.

flashcards.front: Why is a distributed store eventually required?
flashcards.back: A single server reaches capacity quickly and cannot hold the required big data.

flashcards.front: What is another name for a distributed key-value store?
flashcards.back: Distributed hash table.

flashcards.front: Define CAP consistency.
flashcards.back: All clients see the same data at the same time regardless of which node they connect to.

flashcards.front: Define CAP availability.
flashcards.back: A client requesting data gets a response even when some nodes are down.

flashcards.front: Define partition tolerance.
flashcards.back: The system continues to operate despite a communication break between nodes.

flashcards.front: What is a CP system?
flashcards.back: Consistency + partition tolerance, sacrificing availability.

flashcards.front: What is an AP system?
flashcards.back: Availability + partition tolerance, sacrificing consistency.

flashcards.front: Why does the chapter say CA is not realistic for distributed applications?
flashcards.back: Network failures are unavoidable, so partition tolerance is required.

flashcards.front: During a network partition, what must a distributed system choose between?
flashcards.back: Consistency and availability.

flashcards.front: What does the CP example do when n3 is partitioned?
flashcards.back: Blocks writes to n1 and n2 to avoid inconsistency, sacrificing availability.

flashcards.front: What does the AP example do?
flashcards.back: Keeps accepting reads and writes, may serve stale data, and syncs later after the partition resolves.

flashcards.front: Which technique partitions the key-value data?
flashcards.back: Consistent hashing.

flashcards.front: What are the two partitioning challenges?
flashcards.back: Even distribution and minimizing movement when nodes are added/removed.

flashcards.front: How does consistent hashing support heterogeneity?
flashcards.back: Higher-capacity servers receive more virtual nodes.

flashcards.front: What does N mean in data replication?
flashcards.back: The configurable number of replicas.

flashcards.front: How are N replicas chosen?
flashcards.back: Walk clockwise from the key position and choose the first N unique physical servers.

flashcards.front: Why must replica selection consider unique physical servers?
flashcards.back: Several virtual nodes may belong to the same physical server.

flashcards.front: Why place replicas in different data centers?
flashcards.back: Nodes in one data center can fail together from power, network, or disaster events.

flashcards.front: What is W?
flashcards.back: The write quorum size: the number of replica acknowledgements required before a write succeeds.

flashcards.front: What is R?
flashcards.back: The read quorum size: the minimum number of replica responses required before a read succeeds.

flashcards.front: Does W=1 mean the system writes to only one replica?
flashcards.back: No. Data can still be replicated to all N; the coordinator simply needs one acknowledgement to return success.

flashcards.front: What does the coordinator do?
flashcards.back: Acts as a proxy between the client and replica nodes.

flashcards.front: What is the quorum latency/consistency tradeoff?
flashcards.back: Small W/R gives faster responses; larger W/R generally improves consistency but requires waiting for more replicas.

flashcards.front: What condition guarantees strong consistency in the chapter?
flashcards.back: W + R > N.

flashcards.front: What configuration is optimized for fast reads?
flashcards.back: R = 1 and W = N.

flashcards.front: What configuration is optimized for fast writes?
flashcards.back: W = 1 and R = N.

flashcards.front: What common strongly consistent configuration is given?
Define strong consistency.
flashcards.back: Reads always return the most recently written value; clients do not see stale data.

flashcards.front: Define weak consistency.
flashcards.back: A later read may not see the newest value.

flashcards.front: Define eventual consistency.
flashcards.back: A weak consistency model in which, given enough time, all updates propagate and replicas converge.

flashcards.front: Which consistency model is recommended for this design?
flashcards.back: Eventual consistency.

flashcards.front: What is versioning?
flashcards.back: Treating each data modification as a new immutable version.

flashcards.front: Why are versions needed?
flashcards.back: Concurrent writes to replicas can produce conflicting values that must be detected and reconciled.

flashcards.front: What is a vector clock?
flashcards.back: A collection of [server, version] pairs associated with a data item.

flashcards.front: What happens when a server already has an entry in the vector clock and writes the item?
flashcards.back: Increment that server's version counter.

flashcards.front: What happens if the writing server has no vector-clock entry?
flashcards.back: Create a new [server, 1] entry.

flashcards.front: What is D2's vector clock in the example?
What are the conflicting descendants of D2?
What is D5 after reconciliation?
When is X an ancestor of Y?
flashcards.back: When Y's corresponding vector-clock counters are all greater than or equal to X's.

flashcards.front: What do sibling versions indicate?
flashcards.back: A conflict.

flashcards.front: What are two vector-clock downsides?
flashcards.back: Client conflict-resolution complexity and rapid growth of [server,version] pairs.

flashcards.front: How is vector-clock growth bounded?
flashcards.back: Set a maximum length and remove the oldest pairs when it is exceeded.

flashcards.front: Why is one node's accusation not enough to mark another node down?
flashcards.back: The chapter says failure should usually be confirmed by at least two independent information sources.

flashcards.front: Why is all-to-all multicasting unattractive?
flashcards.back: It is inefficient when there are many servers.

flashcards.front: What does each node maintain for gossip failure detection?
flashcards.back: A membership list with member IDs and heartbeat counters.

flashcards.front: What marks a node as offline in gossip?
flashcards.back: Its heartbeat has not increased for longer than a predefined period and other nodes confirm the stale information.

flashcards.front: What is sloppy quorum?
flashcards.back: Use the first W healthy servers for writes and first R healthy servers for reads while ignoring offline servers.

flashcards.front: What is hinted handoff?
flashcards.back: A healthy server temporarily handles data for a failed replica and returns the data when the replica recovers.

flashcards.front: Which failure type is hinted handoff for?
flashcards.back: Temporary failures.

flashcards.front: What handles permanent replica inconsistencies?
flashcards.back: Anti-entropy with Merkle trees.

flashcards.front: What is the main purpose of a Merkle tree here?
flashcards.back: Detect inconsistent portions of replicas and minimize the amount of data transferred during synchronization.

flashcards.front: What are the four Merkle-tree construction steps?
flashcards.back: Bucketize key space, hash keys, make one hash per bucket, then build the tree upward by hashing children.

flashcards.front: How are two Merkle trees compared?
flashcards.back: Compare root hashes, then recursively descend only into differing child hashes/buckets.

flashcards.front: What determines Merkle-tree synchronization volume?
flashcards.back: The differences between replicas, not the total amount of stored data.

flashcards.front: How do you survive a complete data-center outage?
flashcards.back: Replicate data across multiple data centers.

flashcards.front: What are the architectural roles of the coordinator and ring?
flashcards.back: The coordinator proxies client requests; nodes are distributed on a consistent-hashing ring.

flashcards.front: Why is there no single point of failure in the architecture?
flashcards.back: The design is decentralized and every node has the same set of responsibilities.

flashcards.front: What is the first step of the write path?
flashcards.back: Persist the write to the commit log.

flashcards.front: What is the second step of the write path?
flashcards.back: Save the data in the memory cache.

flashcards.front: When is memory data flushed to disk?
flashcards.back: When the memory cache is full or reaches a predefined threshold.

flashcards.front: What is an SSTable?
flashcards.back: A sorted list of <key,value> pairs.

flashcards.front: What is checked first on the read path?
flashcards.back: The memory cache.

flashcards.front: What is the Bloom filter used for?
flashcards.back: To identify which SSTables might contain the key.

flashcards.front: What techniques provide highly available reads in Table 6-2?
flashcards.back: Data replication and multi-data-center setup.

flashcards.front: What techniques provide highly available writes in Table 6-2?
flashcards.back: Versioning and conflict resolution with vector clocks.

flashcards.front: What technique provides tunable consistency?
flashcards.back: Quorum consensus.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does the chapter move from a single server to a distributed key-value store?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: An in-memory hash table is fast, and compression plus hot/cold separation can extend capacity, but a single machine still reaches its space limit quickly. Supporting big data therefore requires partitioning the data across many servers.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain CAP in the context of a network partition.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Partition tolerance is required because network failures are unavoidable. When nodes cannot communicate, the system must choose whether to preserve consistency by rejecting/blocking some operations or preserve availability by continuing to serve operations even if replicas temporarily diverge.

short_answer_questions.question: How does consistent hashing solve data-partitioning requirements?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It distributes keys around a ring so they are assigned to servers by clockwise lookup, helping spread data evenly and minimizing movement when nodes are added or removed. Virtual-node counts can also reflect heterogeneous server capacity.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain N, W, and R.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: N is the number of replicas. W is the number of acknowledgements required for a successful write. R is the number of replica responses required for a successful read. Their values tune latency and consistency.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does W+R>N provide strong consistency in this model?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The read and write quorums must overlap on at least one replica, so a read quorum includes a node that has the latest write.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does the chapter prefer eventual consistency?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Strong consistency can block operations until replicas agree, which hurts high availability. Eventual consistency allows temporary divergence and later convergence, with conflicts handled through versioning and reconciliation.

short_answer_questions.question: How does a vector clock detect conflict?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Each version carries per-server counters. If one vector is entirely less than or equal to another, it is an ancestor and there is no conflict. If the vectors contain incomparable progress—one has a higher counter for one participant and a lower counter for another—they are siblings and conflict.

short_answer_questions.question: How does gossip protocol detect failure?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Nodes maintain membership lists and heartbeat counters, increment and propagate heartbeats to random peers, update membership from received data, and mark a member offline when its heartbeat fails to advance for a predefined period and the stale state is corroborated.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare hinted handoff and Merkle-tree repair.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Hinted handoff is for temporary failures: a healthy node serves/stores on behalf of the failed replica and hands data back after recovery. Merkle trees support anti-entropy for more durable inconsistencies by identifying only differing replica regions for synchronization.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the local write path.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The node first persists the write to a commit log, then writes it to memory cache. Once the memory cache reaches a threshold, the data is flushed to an on-disk SSTable.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the local read path on a cache miss.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: After memory cache misses, the node checks a Bloom filter to determine which SSTables may contain the key, retrieves the result from the relevant SSTables, and returns the value to the client.

common_confusions.confusion: W=1 means only one copy of the data is written.
common_confusions.correction: W=1 means only one acknowledgement is required before the write is considered successful; replication can still occur across N replicas.

common_confusions.confusion: CA is a practical distributed-system choice during real network failures.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter says partition tolerance is required because network failures are unavoidable, so real distributed designs choose between CP and AP behavior.
Strong consistency can block operations and reduce availability; the chapter recommends eventual consistency for this design.

common_confusions.confusion: Vector clocks automatically merge application values.
common_confusions.correction: Vector clocks detect ancestry/conflicts, but the chapter says the client still needs conflict-resolution logic.

common_confusions.confusion: A single server can declare another server failed.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter says at least two independent sources are usually needed before marking a node down.

common_confusions.confusion: Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff are for permanent data divergence.
common_confusions.correction: They are used for temporary failures; anti-entropy and Merkle trees are used for persistent replica repair.

common_confusions.confusion: Merkle-tree repair compares and transfers the complete database every time.
common_confusions.correction: The tree narrows comparison to differing branches/buckets so synchronization volume is proportional to the differences.

common_confusions.confusion: The read path checks all SSTables first.
common_confusions.correction: It checks memory first; on a miss, the Bloom filter identifies which SSTables might contain the key.

must_memorize: Key-value store: unique key -> opaque value.
APIs: put(key,value), get(key).
Requirements: <10KB pairs, big data, high availability/scalability, automatic scaling, tunable consistency, low latency.
Single-server optimizations: compression and hot-in-memory/cold-on-disk.
CAP: consistency, availability, partition tolerance.
Real distributed systems must tolerate partitions, so partition-time tradeoff is CP versus AP.
Partition with consistent hashing; higher-capacity servers can receive more virtual nodes.
Replication factor N; choose first N unique physical servers clockwise.
Replicate across data centers for reliability.
W = write quorum, R = read quorum.
W+R>N gives strong consistency in the chapter's model.
R=1,W=N optimizes reads; W=1,R=N optimizes writes.
Recommended model: eventual consistency.
Conflicts: immutable versions + vector clocks.
Vector clocks detect ancestor versus sibling/conflict relationships.
Gossip protocol detects failures using heartbeat counters.
Temporary failures: sloppy quorum + hinted handoff.
Permanent failures: anti-entropy + Merkle tree.
Data-center outage: cross-data-center replication.
Architecture is decentralized; coordinator proxies client operations.
Write path: commit log -> memory cache -> SSTable.
Read path: memory cache -> Bloom filter -> SSTables -> client.
